page: Amazon Web Services r7g.large is a memory-optimized virtual machine instance powered by custom 64-bit ARM-based AWS Graviton3 processors. Built on the Nitro hypervisor, this instance features 2 dedicated physical cores and 2 vCPUs running at 2.6 GHz with a Neoverse-V1 microarchitecture. It is equipped with 16.0 GB of system memory, yielding a high memory-to-vCPU ratio of 8.0 GB per core. The processor includes 64 KB L1d cache, 1.0 MB L2 cache, and 32 MB L3 cache. There is no local NVMe storage or GPU hardware included, requiring network-attached storage for persistent volumes.

Benchmark data indicates a clear distinction between single-core and multi-core performance. The r7g.large achieves average single-core performance, with a stress-ng single-core score of 1532.49 and a Geekbench single-core score of 1452.0. However, multi-core performance is relatively weak, scoring 3040.96 in stress-ng multi-core and 2589.0 in Geekbench multi-core. Memory performance is mixed; while the large-block uncached read bandwidth is average at 53.89 GB/sec, the write bandwidth is weak at 20.68 GB/sec. Additionally, cryptographic and extended instruction tests show poor performance, with a Passmark CPU encryption score of 272.63.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the ARM64 architecture provides a resource-dense memory profile at a lower qualitative cost compared to traditional x86 memory-optimized instances. The instance is best suited for memory-intensive workloads that do not require heavy parallel CPU scaling or advanced vector instructions. Appropriate use cases include caching layers like Redis, lightweight database operations, text processing, and general-purpose applications requiring a larger memory footprint relative to compute capacity.

Performance benchmarks reveal average single-core capabilities, with a Geekbench single-core score of 1452.0, alongside average large-block memory read speeds of 53.89 GB/sec. However, multi-core scaling and cryptographic operations are weak, as shown by a Passmark CPU score of 1568.48. This hardware profile offers a cost-efficient memory footprint for workloads that prioritize RAM capacity over parallel compute power.
